analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to affirmatively approve every major federal regulation before it can take effect.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2024 with 7 Republican cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would flip how federal regulations work: today, a major agency rule takes effect after public comment and review, and Congress can vote to cancel it. Under this bill, no major rule — any rule costing the economy $100 million or more, plus many agency guidance documents — could take effect unless both chambers of Congress pass a law approving it within 70 legislative days. If Congress simply does nothing, the rule dies. It also exempts deregulatory actions from any vote, sunsets every approved rule after 10 years, and lets companies escape a rule in court if the underlying statute was unclear. The bill was referred to three House committees and received no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Large regulated industries — polluters, manufacturers, financial firms, and other businesses facing major federal rules — gain the most if it passes, because almost no major rule would survive the requirement that both chambers affirmatively pass a law approving it. They would also keep any rules already in place weaker, since every major rule expires after 10 years unless Congress re-approves it, and they could sidestep rules in court by arguing the underlying law was too vague to put them on notice.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large regulated industries facing federal rules

how_it_helps.text: Major federal rules — roughly, any rule with $100 million or more in annual economic effect — would have no legal force unless both chambers of Congress enact a joint resolution approving the rule within 70 session or legislative days; if Congress does not act, the rule is 'deemed not to be approved' and never takes effect.
Rules identified as deregulatory actions are exempt from the approval process entirely, so removing protections requires no vote while adding them does.

Every approved major rule would automatically expire 10 years later, and agencies could not reissue substantially the same rule without a new act of Congress, forcing periodic re-litigation of existing protections.

The bill extends the approval requirement to 'significant guidance documents' and creates a private right of action letting regulated parties challenge an agency's classification of a rule, plus an affirmative defense letting a defendant escape a rule if a person of ordinary intelligence could not have anticipated from the statute that the conduct was unlawful.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people bear the cost as unissued rules leave them exposed: workplace safety standards, clean air and water limits, food safety, consumer financial protections, and auto safety rules that agencies develop would need 535 votes to survive, and in practice most would die by congressional inaction. Consumers and workers would also face a harder time enforcing rules, since the bill lets violators argue the underlying law was too vague to make their conduct clearly illegal.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers, consumers, and communities relying on federal rules

drawbacks.text: The bill's core mechanism means regulation by inaction: because Congress routinely leaves hundreds of measures unvoted, most major rules — including public health, environmental, and consumer protections — would simply never take effect, and the emergency exception lets a rule run for only 90 days even when the President declares an imminent threat to health or safety.

Proponents argue Congress, not unelected agencies, should make law, and that forcing a recorded vote increases accountability; supporters also point to the bill's transparency provisions, such as requiring agencies to publish the data and cost-benefit analyses behind rules and to post guidance documents online.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated goal — elected lawmakers accountable for major rules — is real, but the design achieves it by giving any chamber's inaction a veto over public protections while requiring no vote at all to strip regulations. The 10-year expiration of every major rule and the vagueness defense for violators go further, effectively dismantling the regulatory system rather than adding a check on it. The cost to health, safety, and consumer protections would fall on people with the least ability to protect themselves individually.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary, Budget, and Rules committees in September 2024, and no committee ever scheduled a hearing or markup on it, so it died without a vote when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Kat Cammack introduced H.R. 9648, the Regulations from the Executive in Need of Scrutiny (REINS) Act of 2024, on September 18, 2024, joined by six original cosponsors.

The bill was referred to the House Committees on the Judiciary, the Budget, and Rules, and the action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the 118th Congress.
Seven House Republicans in total cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.

Under the bill's text, a major rule could take effect only if Congress enacted a joint resolution of approval within 70 session or legislative days, and the rule would be 'deemed not to be approved' otherwise.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the existing system stayed in place: federal agencies' major rules continue to take effect after public review without needing a new act of Congress, and the public kept the protections that would have been subject to expiration and congressional veto. The regulated industries that sought the change gained nothing in this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on federal health and safety rules

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 7 cosponsors were House Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached a floor vote in either chamber.

industries.industry: Large regulated corporations generally (manufacturers, energy, chemicals, utilities)
industries.note: The bill would let them avoid most new major rules by default, since rules die unless both chambers affirmatively approve them, and would sunset existing major rules after 10 years. Their gain comes directly from rules protecting workers, consumers, and the environment not taking effect.

Major consumer financial rules — including significant guidance documents — would need congressional approval to take effect, and the vagueness defense would give regulated parties a new way to defeat enforcement actions. Ordinary consumers would face weaker recourse against predatory practices.

industries.industry: Regulatory Affairs and OMB oversight office (Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs)
industries.note: The bill routes all major-rule classification and the annual regulatory budget through OIRA and the OMB Director, expanding that office's gatekeeping role. This centralizes power in a White House office rather than science-based agencies.

Agencies would lose the ability to issue major rules that bind without a new act of Congress, and their rules would face expiration, classification challenges, and private lawsuits. This is the mechanism by which public protections would be weakened.
